chapter.title: A Standard for Everyone
chapter.sub: Four hundred rooms, seven years, five people who didn't write it.
chapter.status: **DRAFT** · scripted from the season map ahead of its production-bible entry · IDs provisional

items.text: SEASON 3 · EPISODE 7 · DRAFT  Design studio · Maya and Avery · Level L3 (Technician)  Four hundred rooms. Seven years. Maya writes the room standard; Avery tests it with five people who didn't write it. The test is humbling. One page nobody tests goes in anyway.  ⚑ RV-71 · RV-72 · RV-73: accessibility content is illustrative and needs specialist and community review. Some choices in this episode run on a clock.

items.title: Five People Who Didn't Write It
items.stakes: Four hundred rooms. Seven years. One document. Whatever's on these pages, people live with.
items.reward: A standard written for people. And one page nobody reviewed.

objectives.text: Put Start where Participant 2 can reach it
Get the remote half onto the loop
Read section 5.3 like a stranger would
Look closer: two things in the test room

items.rumor: Somewhere in the draft is a page that worked once, at one in the morning, in a field.

items.sub: Tuesday · 9:02 a.m. · Juniper Room, the pilot room for the new standard

items.alt: The Juniper Room. The wall display is black. The touch panel on the table reads PRESENTATION SOURCE. A vice-president, arms up in frustration, holds the end of the table cable she has just pulled out of her laptop.

bubbles.text: It's broken. I pressed it. Nothing. I'll just email everyone the deck.

items.caption: Participant 1 runs a budget the size of a small town (illustrative). Four seconds of black screen beat her.

items.alt: Behind the observation glass, Maya is halfway out of her chair. Avery, clipboard in hand, doesn't move.

bubbles.text: It isn't broken — it's switching! Let me just—
Don't help. Watch. Write down what she tried and what she expected.

items.caption: Avery's first rule: the four hundred rooms won't have you in them.

lines.text: It isn't broken — it's switching! Let me just—
(It is physically painful not to help.)

items.prompt: 9:02:06. Participant 1 has pulled the cable and is reaching for her phone to email the deck. What do you do?
items.happening: A first-time user thinks the room is broken. It isn't — it's silent.
known: ◉ She pulled the cable at 4 s
items.risk: Every first-time user in four hundred rooms.
timeout: While you hesitate, Maya bursts in and plugs the cable back in herself. The finding walks out with the VP.
Doing nothing on purpose is a skill. Doing nothing by accident isn't.

hints.text: The room won't have you in it.
A test is for learning what fails, not for rescuing the session.

options.label: Go in and show her it works
options.result: You walk in, plug it back, wait six seconds. “See?” She nods politely.
options.consequence: You rescued one meeting and lost the finding. Four hundred rooms still go black for six seconds.
options.fail: You contaminated the test. The design failed; you covered for it.

options.label: Stay quiet. Note what she tried and when. Afterward, ask what she expected
options.result: Avery's notes: tapped at 0.0, black, pulled cable at 4.0. Afterward: “I thought I'd broken the room. I always think I've broken the room.”
options.consequence: A finding you can design against.

options.label: Pause the session and relabel the button right now
options.result: You stick a label saying SHARE over the old text. The next participant taps SHARE — and gets six seconds of black.
options.consequence: You fixed the word, not the silence.
options.fail: You changed the design mid-test before you understood what failed.

options.label: Use the intercom: “It's working, just wait!”
options.result: She waits. It works. She's embarrassed.
options.consequence: You learned she can wait when told. Nobody will tell her in room 212.
options.fail: You defended the design instead of testing it.

items.alt: After the task, the VP sits back and explains to Avery, who takes notes.

bubbles.text: I pressed it, it went black, so I assumed I'd broken the room. I always assume I've broken the room.
That's the most useful sentence anyone's said about this panel.

lines.text: I always assume I've broken the room.
Most useful sentence anyone's said about this panel. I'm getting it framed.

items.alt: Maya's monitor shows the draft room standard, version 0.9: room types, audio, video, control, network — and an empty accessibility section. Imani stands beside the desk.

bubbles.text: Steering committee Friday. The refresh goes to bid Monday. Whatever's on those pages, four hundred rooms live with for seven years.
No pressure, then.

items.caption: Three hundred rooms today, a hundred on the new floors. One document.

items.alt: Nora at the next desk, pointing at an inventory screen: 289 standard rooms, 100 on new floors, 11 exceptions found, exception owners unknown.

bubbles.text: The standard's supposed to end exceptions. Just remember eleven rooms still aren't on any list but mine.

items.caption: The eleven rooms from the green dashboard. The boardroom is one of them.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #28 · AVERY'S LENS  Design for the edges  Design for people at the edges — reach, hearing, sight — and the middle benefits too (the curb-cut effect).  A panel within seated reach and a real listening mix help a wheelchair user and a hearing-aid user — and everyone in a hurry.

items.alt: Avery has written five participants on the whiteboard: a VP who never touches tech, a wheelchair user from Legal, a hearing-aid user from Finance, a new hire on day three, and Sam from IT.

bubbles.text: You can't test what you wrote. You already know where the buttons are. Five people who didn't write it will find most of what's wrong.

items.caption: Five is a rule of thumb for finding problems, not proof they're all found.

items.alt: System View timeline of Participant 1's four seconds: she taps at 0.0; the display changes input at 0.3; from 0.3 to 6.0 seconds it resyncs, black, with no message; she pulls the cable at 4.0. The panel said only 'Presentation Source' the whole time. The room was switching correctly; content would have appeared at 6.0 seconds.
items.caption: The room did its job. It just didn't say so.

items.title: The button worked
items.body: Everyone blamed the label. Avery's timeline shows the Share button worked perfectly — the display needed six seconds to resync and said nothing while it did. The VP didn't fail to find Share. She found it, pressed it, and believed the silence. Look back at the cold open: a black screen, a panel that never changed, and a stopwatch at 00:04.
items.label: Test: reason from the timeline. What failed, and what requirement goes in the standard?

items.alt: Avery's redesigned panel mock-up: one big SHARE button and a green progress bar reading 'Connecting your screen… 3'.

bubbles.text: Finding one: the button worked, the room didn't say so. Now it counts down. People will wait for a countdown.

items.caption: The panel rewrite began with a stopwatch, not a style guide.

items.alt: At the Juniper Room's door, a wall panel is mounted high beside the frame. Participant 2, a lawyer who uses a wheelchair, reaches toward it; her fingertips reach its lower corner. Avery watches from the doorway, writing.

bubbles.text: I can reach the corner. Is Start in the corner? It's never in the corner.

items.caption: Participant 2 has tested more buildings than anyone on the project. She's funnier about it than they deserve.

items.prompt: Is Start in the corner? It's never in the corner. Go on, tell me it's “accessible.”

options.label: “Show me where you'd look for it. We'll put it there.”
options.reply: …Oh. Nobody's ever asked. Down here. Obviously.

options.label: “It meets the height guideline.”
options.reply: The guideline has never tried to join a meeting at 8:59.

options.label: “We'll look into it.”
options.reply: That's what the last three buildings said.

items.prompt: The door panel is above Participant 2's reach. What does the standard say?
items.happening: The control people need is above one participant's reach.
known: ◉ Table-panel option in the pilot kit

options.label: Keep the height; add a note: “a colleague can assist”
options.result: Avery puts her pen down. Participant 2: “So I book rooms I can't start.”
options.consequence: A room one of your colleagues can't operate alone.
options.fail: Needing to ask for help to start your own meeting isn't access.

options.label: A table panel on a cable within seated reach, plus a wall panel lowered into reach, both tested with her
options.result: Participant 2 finds Share at the table without looking up; the wall panel starts the room from the door.
options.consequence: Everyone uses the table panel more, it turns out.

options.label: Remove panels; everything from people's laptops
options.result: Participant 1 has no idea how to start the room from her laptop. Neither does the new hire.
options.consequence: You traded one exclusion for three.
options.fail: Designing for the people in the room who already know how.

options.label: Add voice control instead
options.result: Untested with anyone. Participant 3's aids pick up the room's voice prompts as echo.
options.consequence: Maybe someday; not a version-1 answer.

items.text: 🔭 PHYSICS IN MOTION  The room hearing-aid users struggle in  The science under this episode’s problem — live.

items.sub: Beginner · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Avery and Maya beside a board. A hearing loop sends sound straight to hearing aids. But if the room rings, everyone struggles first. How long does this room ring? Sabine again: point-one-six-one times volume over absorption. Two hundred cubic metres, forty of absorption: about point eight seconds.

bubbles.text: A hearing loop sends sound straight to hearing aids. But if the room rings, everyone struggles first.
How long does this room ring?
Sabine again: point-one-six-one times volume over absorption. Two hundred cubic metres, forty of absorption: about point eight seconds.

items.caption: Beginner: the term, what it means, the formula — and one worked example out loud.

items.text: 📘 RAY'S NOTEBOOK · BEGINNER  Terms    Reverberation   Sound persisting in a room after the source stops, from many reflections.   Room standard   The written specification every meeting room follows.   Hearing loop   An assistive listening system that sends audio magnetically to hearing aids.   Formula, variables and a worked example   ƒ FORMULA · Sabine reverberation time  RT 60  = 0.161 × V ÷ A   RT 60   time for sound to fall 60 dB, s  V  room volume, m³  A  total absorption, m² (sabins)    Worked example.  A 500 m³ room with 50 m² of absorption: 0.161 × 500 ÷ 50 ≈ 1.6 s.
📒 EMPATHIA LEARN FIELDBOOK · MODULE 28 OF 31 · PP. 89–96, 99, 127  PART 6 ROOM PHYSICS & COVERAGE  Page 127:  Honor the message by making it accessible.  Maya had circled it once, and then again.

items.label: **Fieldbook module 28 — Coverage and intelligibility — point it at people.** Beginner support: every new word is defined, and every formula comes with its variables and a worked example.

items.text: 📖 From the Fieldbook · module 28 · tap a plate to open it full size     Audio coverage, room physics and vocal control     Speaker aim, center fill and coverage     Speaker aim matters     Speaker aiming matters — same system, different aim

items.alt: At the table, Participant 2 has the table panel within reach; the display shows her forecast slide. The panel reads SHARE, connected.

bubbles.text: Found it. Didn't even have to look up. Put that in your standard.

items.caption: The table panel went into every room type. The people who use it most don't use a wheelchair.

items.alt: System View, top view of the Juniper Room: an oval table with twelve seats. Two ceiling microphone zones cover the near and middle seats; three seats at the far end, near the screen, fall outside every zone and are marked red. A note: the far end hears those seats as distant, roomy and quiet.
items.caption: Remote people said the far end of the table “sounds like it's in a stairwell.” It is, acoustically.

items.teaser: the far end of the table
items.title: A stairwell, acoustically
items.body: Remote people have been saying it for years. The tickets are all tagged *subjective.* Avery tags them *correct.*

items.title: Georg von Békésy and the cochlea
items.body: Georg von Békésy won the 1961 Nobel Prize for showing how the cochlea sorts sound by frequency along a travelling wave. Hearing loss often narrows that sorting — which is why long reverberation, a nuisance for most, can make speech unreadable for some.

items.alt: Participant 3, from Finance, listens with a hand behind her ear; a small hearing aid is drawn behind it. Two remote colleagues are talking on the display. Maya watches from the side of the room.

bubbles.text: On the loop I hear this room perfectly. The two on the screen — nothing. Just their mouths moving.
…The loop only gets the room mics.

items.caption: Maya has heard this sentence before, in a sanctuary, from a woman in row 8.

items.prompt: The loop carries room microphones only. The meeting's remote half is silent for her. Fix it — the session ends in two minutes.
items.happening: The listening loop is fed from the room-mic mix only.
known: ◉ Far-end audio goes to loudspeakers only
items.risk: Every hearing-aid user in every hybrid meeting.
timeout: The session ends with Participant 3 lip-reading two people on a screen.
A two-minute fix, left undone, becomes seven years of rooms.

options.label: Turn the room loudspeakers up
options.result: The room gets loud. The echo canceller struggles; remote people hear themselves. Her loop still carries nothing from the far end.
options.fail: You made the room worse for everyone and fixed nothing for her.

options.label: Switch the loop to a listening mix: far-end audio plus room speech, saved in every preset
options.result: She switches her aid to the loop program. “There they are.”
options.consequence: An output with its own intent — and a line in the standard.

options.label: Offer her a transcript after the meeting
options.result: She'll read tomorrow what everyone else heard today.
options.consequence: Access, delayed, is still exclusion from the conversation.

options.label: Suggest she sits closer to the loudspeaker
options.result: Closer to the loudspeaker, further from the loop's best spot. And further from her team.
options.consequence: Moving the person instead of the signal.
options.fail: The room's job is to reach her seat, not choose it.

items.alt: Participant 3 smiles; the two remote colleagues are talking on the display. Avery, beside her, writes.

bubbles.text: There they are. Both of them. I'd stopped expecting to hear remote people in meetings.

items.caption: Stopped expecting it. Maya writes that phrase at the top of the accessibility section.

evidence.label: loop · far end + room · her seat

lines.text: I'd stopped expecting to hear remote people in meetings.

items.alt: Participant 5: Sam, grinning, has already shared a slide in two seconds. Avery doesn't look impressed.

bubbles.text: Two seconds. Beat that.
Your result doesn't count. You built half of it.

items.label: **Learn it now:** speech intelligibility and microphone coverage — distance, zones, and the listening feed.
**Route it:** every voice to every ear.

items.alt: Late at night in the dark office, the whiteboard lists version-1 items: reach and loop as musts; feedback, coverage, fallback card and guards as questions; giant screens and voice control crossed out. Imani and Maya face it.

bubbles.text: We can't buy all of it in version one. Pick what retires the most risk, and say out loud what we're leaving out.
That sentence sounds like Tasha.

items.caption: Every figure on that board is illustrative. The choosing is real.

items.label: **Triage:** you have the budget line. What goes into version 1?

items.alt: Midnight. Nora leans over Maya's shoulder, pointing at the network section on her screen.

bubbles.text: Section 5.3. “Room devices: fixed addresses at the top of each range.” Where's that from?
Riverbend. The festival. Priya talked me through it at one in the morning. It worked.

items.caption: Nora nods and scrolls on. It's late, and it worked.

lines.text: (Nora nods and scrolls on. It's late, and it worked.)

items.alt: Close-up of a printed page: Room Standard version 1.0, section 5, Network. Line 5.3 reads: Room devices: fixed addresses at the top of each automatic range. Proven at Riverbend. The page glows faintly.
items.caption: *This page will be copied into four hundred rooms.*

items.title: “Room devices: fixed addresses at the top of each range.”
items.body: No reference. No reason. No owner. Just a rule that sounds like it came from somewhere. It did: a napkin, in a field, at 1 a.m., which is now in a landfill.

items.title: The page that worked
items.body: You've seen this page before — at 1 a.m. at Riverbend, when Maya gave festival equipment fixed addresses at the top of the range without excluding them from automatic assignment. It worked because the site was small. Nobody wrote it down then. Tonight it's written down for the first time — as a rule for four hundred rooms. Nobody in the room notices. You did.
items.label: Test: reason from what you know that they don't. Why did it work, and what will it do at scale?

items.alt: The steering committee in a meeting room. On the display: Room Standard v1.0 — five people, three rooms, forty-one tests, within the budget line. Imani presents; the finance lead holds the printed budget.

bubbles.text: Every requirement on that page has a test and a person who failed without it.
And every one has a price. Which ones are the extras?

items.caption: Friday, 10:12. Eighteen minutes of agenda.

items.prompt: Friday. The steering committee. The finance lead: “Can we hit the number by cutting the accessibility items?” You have the floor.
items.happening: The committee wants the number. Two items are commitments.
known: ▮ V1 fits the budget with commitments first (illustrative)
items.risk: Four hundred rooms and everyone who books them.
timeout: The finance lead fills the silence: “Let's trim the extras.” The loop feed and table panels go first.
In a budget meeting, silence is a vote for the cheapest line.

hints.text: Commitments first. Then risk per dollar. Then say what you're not doing.

options.label: Cut the table panels and the loop feed to hit the number
options.result: The budget closes. Participants 2 and 3 will book rooms they can't use for seven years.
options.consequence: The cheapest items retire the most exclusion.
options.fail: Those were commitments. The test proved who pays for cutting them.

options.label: Ship version 1: tested requirements only, commitments first, risk per dollar — and a named, dated list of what's deferred
options.result: The committee reads one page: each requirement, its test, its cost, its owner. The deferred list has dates.
options.consequence: Approved. Version 1.0 goes to bid Monday.

options.label: Delay the standard a quarter to include everything
options.result: The refresh goes to bid Monday anyway — on the old standard.
options.consequence: Four hundred rooms bought on the document you meant to replace.
options.fail: Perfect next quarter loses to good enough today.

options.label: Adopt a vendor's reference design wholesale
options.result: It's thorough. It has never met Participant 1, 2 or 3.
options.consequence: A standard written for someone else's building.
options.fail: You threw away the only evidence you had: five real people.

items.label: **Service Mode:** 9:56, the pilot room, three people who couldn't use it yesterday. Four minutes.

items.alt: The approved Room Standard v1.0 cover page: tested with five people in three rooms. Share shows progress within about a second; controls within seated reach; loop fed by far end plus room; mic coverage checked at every seat by ear; section 3.4, two content inputs — table and wall; deferred items with owners and dates.
items.caption: Section 3.4 exists because of Participant 2: a content input at the table, one at the wall.

items.alt: Friday afternoon. Avery packs her clipboard.

bubbles.text: You didn't write a standard for rooms. You wrote one for people.
You wrote half of it. And Participant 2 wrote the best line.

items.alt: Evening at the service desk. Sam stares at his queue: Garden Room, display on the wrong input, closed eight times with the same fix — and opened again at 7:14 this morning.

bubbles.text: I've closed this ticket nine times.

items.caption: Next: *Ticket Closed.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Test a standard with people who didn't write it, and don't help them. A button that works silently fails in the user's mind: show progress. Put controls where every participant can reach them. Feed the listening system with the far end as well as the room, and check microphone coverage seat by seat from the far end. Scope version 1 by risk, commitments first, and name what you left out. And never let “it worked” into a standard without a review by the owner of what it touches.

REFLECTION (optional)  · Three people told Maya the room didn't work for them, and each said it kindly. One page nobody questioned said the opposite. Which kind of evidence did you trust more this week?  Boundary: this reflection doesn't prove anything about the rooms.
